approved: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
The bill would provide extra money in 2014 to schools that educate many Indigenous students who board and come from distant regions.
It would stop funding reductions for students with disabilities and those in certain independent special schools by aligning their transition rules with other schools.
The bill would fix mistakes in the Australian Education Act 2013 that cause uncertainty for schools.
The bill creates the Indigenous Boarding Initiative, worth about $6.8 million, for eligible schools.
The bill ensures transitional funding for some special schools matches the rules for other schools.
The bill corrects errors in the original Act that affect funding and regulation.
Schools with Indigenous boarding students from remote areas, students with disabilities, and independent special schools are affected.

Reported that the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Human Rights had assessed 11 bills, found 10 did not require further scrutiny, deferred consideration of five and sought further information on the National Security Legislation Amendment Bill (No. 1) 2014, including its effects on specified human rights.

Opposed parts of the Australian Education Amendment Bill, supporting $6.8 million in 2014-15 funding for boarding schools with large numbers of remote Indigenous students, but condemned the government for cutting the $100 million More Support for Students with Disabilities program and failing to deliver the promised full Gonski disability loading from 2015.

Supported the Australian Education Amendment Bill, explaining it provides about $6.8 million for schools with large numbers of remote Indigenous boarding students, prevents funding cuts to students with disabilities at independent special schools that would otherwise start on 1 January 2015, and defended the government's four-year school funding commitment covering 2014 to 2017.

Criticized the government's $6.8 million Indigenous boarding initiative as inadequate against broader Indigenous funding cuts, citing budget papers showing a $534.4 million cut to Indigenous programs, and accused the government of cutting $30 billion from school funding over the next decade by adopting CPI indexation from 2018 and abandoning the fifth and sixth years of Gonski funding.

Supported the Australian Education Amendment Bill, describing how two schools in her electorate of Durack would benefit from the $6.8 million Indigenous boarding initiative, Karalundi Aboriginal Education Community near Meekatharra, established in 1954 and catering for up to 60 boarding students, and the Yiramalay/Wesley Studio School partnership with 40 Aboriginal students enrolled in 2014.

Supported the Australian Education Amendment Bill 2014, highlighting $6.8 million in funding under the Indigenous Boarding Initiative to address a resourcing shortfall at boarding schools with large numbers of Indigenous students.

Supported the Australian Education Amendment Bill's provisions correcting funding anomalies for students with disabilities in independent schools, highlighting Giant Steps, an autism-specific school in Deloraine, Tasmania, that has run for nearly 20 years, teaching 26 full and part-time students alongside 15 children in early intervention and eight adult clients.

Argued against the Australian Education Amendment Bill's approach to Indigenous boarding schools, saying the government halted a contracted boarding facility at Garrthalala in North-East Arnhem Land despite a KPMG feasibility study recommending the site, and said the Remote School Attendance Strategy has cost $46 million while boosting attendance by only six per cent in some terms.

Argued in support of the Australian Education Amendment Bill's funding for Indigenous boarding schools, recounting a visit to an APY Lands community where hearing tests found only three good ears out of 260 students, and praised a direct instruction literacy program being introduced in 200 communities next year.

Argued that Labor would support the Australian Education Amendment Bill's $6.8 million funding for Indigenous boarding schools and its fix to stop about 38 schools facing funding cuts in 2015, but accused the minister of delaying school improvement plans to January 2016 as a way to unwind the Gonski school funding agreement.

Argued in the debate on the Australian Education Amendment Bill for a more bipartisan approach to education, criticising the previous government for cutting $2.3 billion from higher education in its last budget, and read a Christmas message calling education the greatest gift Australia can give its children.

Disputed Labor's claims of education funding cuts, citing ABC Fact Check's finding that the government did not cut $30 billion from schools, and said Commonwealth funding to New South Wales public schools would rise 49.6 per cent by 2017 to 2018 compared with Labor's last budget, while the bill also provides $6.8 million for schools with large numbers of remote Indigenous boarding students.

Supported measures providing about $6.8 million for Indigenous boarding schools and protecting independent special-school funding, but opposed delaying school improvement plans and argued that cuts to Gonski and $100 million in disability support would disadvantage students.

Supported amendments providing approximately $6.8 million through the Indigenous Boarding Initiative, $2.4 million for certain schools and a corrected funding formula, and argued that education policy should improve attendance, parental engagement, teacher quality, opportunity and outcomes for Indigenous students.

Supported the bill's three components, including around $6.8 million for boarding schools, protection for independent special schools and delaying school improvement plans, but argued that the measures reflected a failure to implement Gonski reforms and reneged on funding and disability-support commitments.

Argued that the Australian Education Amendment Bill 2014 responded to broken Gonski commitments and education cuts, while supporting Indigenous boarding schools, continued funding for independent special schools, delayed school-improvement plans and $6.8 million for eligible boarding schools.

Argued that the bill supported boarding schools and independent special schools but reflected broken commitments on Gonski funding, disability loading and school accountability, and urged restoration of years 5 and 6 funding and the $100 million disability program.

Supported amendments enabling the Indigenous Boarding Initiative, describing its eligibility criteria and around $6.8 million in additional funding, while also citing Northern Territory school funding, special-school support, delayed planning requirements and other technical changes.

Argued in support of the Australian Education Amendment Bill 2014, which funds the Indigenous Boarding Initiative with $6.8 million across 21 eligible non-government boarding schools, noting almost 3,000 Indigenous students were enrolled as boarders last year, and welcomed $2.4 million to protect special school funding in 2015.

Argued that the Australian Education Amendment Bill 2014 is only needed because the government abandoned Labor's Gonski reforms, part of an $80 billion cut to schools and hospitals over the next decade, and warned it failed to extend $100 million a year in disability transition funding, while noting Australia's 3.6 million schoolchildren face one of the largest declines in maths among OECD countries since 2000.

Argued in support of the Australian Education Amendment Bill 2014, drawing on his own experience as a scholarship student at the Swanleigh Hostel decades earlier, now used by La Salle College to board Indigenous students from Balgo, and recalled the Aboriginal Secondary Grants scheme established in 1972 that first enabled Aboriginal children to attend boarding schools.

Summed up debate on the Australian Education Amendment Bill 2014, reporting that only one-quarter of Northern Territory children attend school at least 80 per cent of the time needed to learn effectively, and touted the Remote School Attendance Strategy's rollout across 73 schools, which lifted attendance by five to 15 percentage points, alongside a record $64.5 billion in school funding over four years.
